California regulators are actively reworking how large data center loads are billed and interconnected as demand grows statewide. Under SB 57 (2025), the California Public Utilities Commission opened a rate-design rulemaking in April 2026 specifically addressing electric rate impacts of data centers and other large transmission-connected loads, an inquiry expected to run roughly two years and examine dedicated data-center tariffs and the risk of costs shifting onto residential and small-business ratepayers. The California Independent System Operator separately published a formal issue paper on large-load interconnection considerations in January 2026, part of an ongoing CAISO regulatory track addressing how data centers and other large loads connect to the state's transmission grid. Santa Clara's municipal utility, Silicon Valley Power, and the broader South Bay grid have absorbed years of hyperscale and colocation growth predating this rulemaking, making Silicon Valley one of the most power-constrained data center submarkets the state regulators are now studying.

NTT's US Global Data Centers footprint spans seven named campuses in total: Ashburn, Virginia at 224 megawatts; Chicago, Illinois at more than 200 megawatts; Dallas, Texas at 160 megawatts; Hillsboro, Oregon at 126 megawatts; Phoenix, Arizona at 240 megawatts; and a combined Sacramento/Santa Clara, California figure of 68 megawatts, totaling roughly 1,118 megawatts or more of disclosed US capacity, per the operator's own locations page.
